claims.text: A competitive market is a market with a high number of buyers and sellers in which each seller is too small to influence the market price on its own: the price is set by demand and supply across the whole market, and a seller who charges noticeably above the going price tends to lose customers to rivals.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The entry of new sellers into a competitive market raises the quantity offered at each price, which tends to pull the market price down and narrow each seller's profit, because buyers can switch freely to a cheaper rival.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The effect of a high number of firms, as buyers meet it, tends to be prices held near costs, steady pressure on sellers to keep quality up, wide choice, and a thin profit for each seller, because customers can move between sellers.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: Twelve salons trade at Katutura's hairdressing rank at about N$60 a haircut with costs of about N$40 a cut; two new salons open and the going price drifts to about N$50, so each salon's profit narrows from about N$20 to about N$10 a cut, since N$60 - N$40 = N$20 and N$50 - N$40 = N$10.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A monopoly is a market with a single dominant seller - in the extreme, the only supplier - protected by barriers to entry, such as a government licence, control of a key input, high set-up costs or an established position, which keep new sellers out.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The characteristics of a monopoly are a single dominant seller, barriers to entry holding newcomers back, the power to set its own price within what buyers will pay, and buyers with few alternatives within reach.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The advantages of a monopoly are that a single large seller may reach a scale that lowers its cost per unit - and part of the saving may reach buyers - and may fund networks that many small sellers could not, while the disadvantages are prices tending above the many-seller level, output and choice held back, weaker pressure on quality where buyers cannot easily switch, and profit staying high behind the barriers.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: The demand curve facing a dominant seller is the market's own demand curve, sloping downward, so a higher price tends to cost it sales; the seller moves along the curve when it changes its price, and the barriers are what let its price sit above the level a market of many small sellers would tend to charge.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.

claims.text: A monopoly's profit, protected by barriers to entry, may fund research and development into new products and methods that small firms could not afford, and the security of its position may make long, costly investment less risky; whether it does so depends on the firm, since the lack of rivals may also leave it under little pressure to innovate.

verification.method: Authored against the 0455 syllabus scope under standard v0.2.0-draft.
